summary: A frequently asked questions document produced by the Internet School Networking group as an introduction to the Internet for teachers, administrators and other school staff. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A beginner's guide to the Internet written for people who work in schools, answering the questions they ask most.

questions: how can schools get on the internet
what is an acceptable use policy for schools
subtitle: A 1996 plain-language Internet primer for teachers and school administrators, written as questions and answers.

tldr.problem: Educators in primary and secondary schools were getting connected to the Internet with little guidance on what it is, what it costs, how to use it in class, or how to keep it safe.
tldr.mechanism: The FYI document answers common questions in five groups: the Internet in education, getting connected, using services, classroom resources and projects, and security and ethics. It adds reading lists, contacts and a glossary.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational document limited to the United States of 1996, with prices, products and services that date it. It obsoletes RFC 1578.

facts.label: Support budget rule
facts.value: Three dollars of support per dollar of hardware and software

today: RFC 1941 is an Informational FYI from May 1996 that obsoletes RFC 1578. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, but its prices, products and contacts describe the United States in 1996.

sections.title: Who the Guide Is For
sections.content:
RFC 1941 is FYI 22, produced by the Internet School Networking (ISN) group in the User Services Area of the IETF. Its audience is educators in primary and secondary schools who are recently connected, who reach the Internet by some means other than a direct connection, or who are just beginning to consider it. It is explicitly limited in focus to the United States.

The authors warn that the Internet is a changing environment and that some listed contacts may disappear. The document renders the earlier FYI 22, RFC 1578, obsolete. If future updates are produced, the RFC number will change again and the FYI number (22) will remain the same.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a how-to book for teachers who are new to the Internet. The authors admit that some things in it will change.

sections.title: Why Bring the Internet into the Classroom
sections.content:
The guide defines the Internet as a worldwide network of smaller networks linked by a common protocol, with almost 5 million computers at the time of writing. It argues that the most important question for a user is not whether they are on the Internet but whether they have access to the services they want.

For classrooms it lists benefits: up-to-the-minute information, original sources a school could not afford to own, contact with experts and other educators, and a shift away from the teacher as sole expert. It insists that the Internet will not replace teachers or books. It also notes that Internet material often lacks the authority of an established publisher and must be judged critically.

The central advice on curriculum is that the Internet must support goals already set, not be an end in itself. Examples include collecting data from many sites, peer review of student work, and email pen-pal programs.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet is like a window onto the whole world for a classroom. It helps teachers teach, but it does not replace them or books.

sections.title: Getting Connected and What It Costs
sections.content:
Section 4 sorts users into four groups and suggests a connection for each. Basic users who go online a few hours a week may be served by a nationwide online service. Heavier basic users may want a text-only shell account from a local Internet Service Provider. Advanced users who want graphical tools or to offer services should consider a SLIP or PPP account. A school network needs a high-speed dedicated line.

For budgeting, the guide quotes 1996 figures: a modem of 14.4 kilobits per second or faster for dial-up, leased lines at $200 per month or more, a CSU/DSU of $600 to $1000, and a router at roughly $1500. It also gives a rule of thumb: for every dollar spent on hardware and software, plan to spend three dollars to support the technology and its users.

It advises asking vendors and ISPs specific questions, such as whether they provide a primary domain name server, register your domain with the InterNIC and supply the IP addresses you need. It recommends one dedicated connection of 56 Kbs or higher for a school with computers in classrooms, the library and laboratories, and putting access where teachers can use it easily.
sections.plainLanguage: Getting online is like choosing a road for your school. A little country lane is cheap, and a big highway costs more but fits many cars. You also need people who know how to drive.

sections.title: The Internet Services of 1996
sections.content:
The guide spends most of its space on the World Wide Web, calling it the tool coming into most prominence, and it explains browsers, URLs, links and HTML. Many of the other services are reachable through the Web. A browser is a client that retrieves documents from Web servers, and every document has a unique address called a URL.

It then describes the other services in a sentence or two each: email and mailing lists, network news (Usenet), FTP, telnet, Gopher, and searching tools such as Archie, Veronica and WAIS. It ends with videoconferencing by MBONE and CU-SeeMe. The guide says FTP is used less by itself because Web browsers and Gopher clients incorporate it.

These descriptions are a snapshot of what the authors considered current in May 1996. The text names Netscape and Mosaic as the two most common graphical Web browsers.
sections.plainLanguage: The Web is the easy front door to the Internet. Behind it are older tools for mail, files, menus and searching, like different rooms in the same big house.

sections.title: Classroom Resources and Projects
sections.content:
Section 6 points teachers to places that gather material for schools: computer information servers, mailing lists, Usenet news groups in the K12 hierarchy, and conferences. It names organizations such as Global SchoolNet, EdWeb, the Consortium for School Networking and NASA's Spacelink and Quest.

Project examples include data gathered from many sites, such as weather patterns, pollutants in water or air, and Monarch butterfly migration. The European Schools Project is described as involving approximately 200 schools in 20 countries. The guide also suggests printed guides and newsletters, and encourages schools to publish their own Web pages. Appendix C collects more project examples.
sections.plainLanguage: Classes in different places can share what they measure and find, like a huge group science project with kids all over the world.

sections.title: Security, Safety and Ethics
sections.content:
On objectionable material, the guide says the most important and effective action is to write clear Acceptable Use Policies (AUPs) with rules and consequences, and to teach the ethics of Internet use. It describes commercial blocking software, proxy servers and caching servers, and supervised access, and admits that none of these technical solutions had proven wholly successful.

On break-ins, it points to the Site Security Handbook (FYI 8) and says to report outside break-ins to the CERT Coordination Center. On viruses, it recommends installing virus protection software on all computers and downloading only from trusted sources. For manners it points to FYI 28, RFC 1855, "Netiquette Guidelines". The formal Security Considerations section of the RFC just refers back to Section 7.
sections.plainLanguage: Schools need clear rules for using the Internet, just like rules for the playground. They also need grown-ups watching and lessons about right and wrong online.
